title: Acute Glomerulonephritis in Paediatrics
subject: Paediatrics
summary: Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is an immune‑mediated inflammation of the glomerulus, often following infection. It presents with haematuria, oedema and hypertension, and requires prompt assessment of renal function and underlying cause.

sections.p: AGN is characterised by sudden onset of glomerular inflammation, usually immune‑complex mediated. Diagnosis rests on clinical features, urinalysis, renal function and, where available, serology.

t.b: Detects red cell casts and proteinuria – confirms glomerular source
Shows rise in GFR; a rise >50% from baseline suggests significant injury
Positive in post‑streptococcal AGN; supports diagnosis when clinical picture fits
Low in post‑streptococcal AGN; normal in other forms
Red cell casts indicate glomerular bleeding

sections.p: Staging guides monitoring and urgency of intervention. The KDIGO acute kidney injury stages are used, with Stage 3 requiring urgent review.
b: Stage 1: Cr 1.5–1.9× baseline or ≥0.3 mg/dL rise
Stage 3: Cr ≥3.0× baseline or Cr ≥4 mg/dL or need for dialysis

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, infections dominate. The hierarchy starts with streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo, then moves to other bacterial, viral and parasitic triggers.

t.b: Confirms streptococcal throat infection – first step if pharyngitis suspected
Identifies streptococcal impetigo source
Screen if risk factors present – HIV can trigger immune complex GN

sections.p: Children often appear suddenly ill with dark urine and swelling. Blood pressure is frequently high, and the child may be irritable or lethargic.

t.b: Detects hypertension; a systolic >95th percentile is a red flag
Rapidly identifies proteinuria and haematuria

sections.p: Tests should answer the ‘who, what, where, why’ of the renal insult. In low‑resource settings, prioritize bedside tests and simple labs.

t.b: Answers: Is there haematuria or proteinuria? A positive red cell count confirms glomerular bleeding
Answers: Is renal function impaired? A rise >50% from baseline indicates significant injury
Answers: Is there recent streptococcal infection? A titre >200 IU/mL supports post‑streptococcal AGN
Answers: Is complement consumed? Low C3 suggests post‑streptococcal AGN

sections.p: Early recognition of life‑threatening complications is vital. Watch for rapidly rising creatinine, pulmonary oedema, severe hypertension and seizures.

t.b: A rise to ≥4 mg/dL or need for dialysis signals imminent failure
Systolic >180 mmHg or diastolic >110 mmHg warrants emergency management

sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger, control hypertension, and support renal function. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs and monitor fluid balance closely.
b: Antibiotics for streptococcal infection (penicillin V or amoxicillin) – first line

t.b: Answers: How to lower blood pressure? It reduces volume and is safe in AGN
Answers: How to manage oedema? It promotes diuresis but avoid over‑diuresis
Answers: Why? They reduce renal perfusion and worsen injury

sections.p: Regular monitoring of blood pressure, urine output and renal function is essential. Prevention focuses on early treatment of infections and vaccination where available.
b: Urine dipstick every 2 weeks until normal

t.b: Answers: Is renal function improving? A decline toward baseline indicates recovery

sections.p: Differential diagnosis includes acute tubular necrosis, post‑renal obstruction and systemic vasculitis.
b: Acute tubular necrosis – no haematuria, more oliguria

t.b: Answers: Are there red cell casts? Their presence favours AGN

sections.p: Low complement can be normal in some infections; ASO titres may be elevated in asymptomatic carriers. Clinical correlation is mandatory.
b: ASO titre may remain high for months post‑infection

t.b: Answers: Does a high titre confirm AGN? No – it only indicates recent streptococcal exposure

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid rise in serum creatinine to ≥4 mg/dL

faq.q: Why is hypertension common in AGN?
faq.a: Immune complex deposition increases vascular permeability and activates renin‑angiotensin system, raising blood pressure.
Mild cases may recover spontaneously, but untreated severe AGN often leads to chronic kidney disease.

faq.q: What is the role of steroids in AGN?
faq.a: Steroids are reserved for rapidly progressive GN or lupus nephritis; they are not routinely used in post‑streptococcal AGN.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a child with suspected AGN and why? — Urine dipstick to confirm haematuria and proteinuria, the hallmark of glomerular injury.
How would you differentiate AGN from acute tubular necrosis on bedside exam? — Presence of red cell casts on microscopy suggests AGN, whereas ATN shows muddy brown granular casts.
A child with AGN develops severe hypertension. What is the first drug you would give and why? — Hydrochlorothiazide; it lowers BP by diuresis and is safe in renal disease.
Why is NSAID use contraindicated in AGN? — NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin‑mediated vasodilation of afferent arterioles, worsening renal perfusion.
What is the significance of a low C3 complement level in a child with haematuria? — It indicates complement consumption typical of post‑streptococcal AGN.
When would you consider dialysis in a child with AGN? — If serum creatinine rises to ≥4 mg/dL, oliguria persists, or fluid overload causes pulmonary oedema.
How does schistosomiasis lead to AGN in endemic areas? — Chronic S. haematobium infection causes immune complex deposition in the glomerulus, triggering inflammation.
What is the most common trigger of AGN in low‑resource settings? — Streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo.
